newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Dollar powers to four-year peaks against yen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dollar powers to four-year peaks against yen.

text.p: The dollar powered to its highest level in over four years on Monday, ripping through 125 yen in Europe as yield differentials between the world's key economies and the start of Japan's fiscal year boosted demand for the currency.
"What is driving the market at the moment are (these) dual considerations," said Julian Fisher, economist at Daiwa Europe.

Fisher said with the end-of-year repatriation of Japanese assets over, the focus has now shifted to the potential for Japanese assets to be diversified as the 1997/98 fiscal year begins and investors bank on fresh U.S. interest rate rises.
The dollar touched a four-year peak of 125.55 yen at about 1230 GMT, well over one-yen up from 124.25 yen in late Europe on Friday.
The dollar also sprinted higher against the mark and stood at about 1.7045 at 1230 GMT.
"It seems fairly plain that there will be at least one more rise in U.S. interest rates at a time when real rates in Japan are set to turn negative," said Daiwa's Fisher.

U.S. interest rates, which rose on March 25 for the first time in two years, have already increased the pull on Japan's cash and analysts said expectations for even higher rates after healthy jobless figures on Friday will contrast with yields in Japan where interest rates are among the world's lowest.
Dollar bulls, said analysts, were also encouraged on Monday by the lack of trade friction caused by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's visit to Japan and his stance on the dollar.
Analysts said the market failed to react to Rubin when he urged Japan to guard against a resurgence in its trade surplus and warned a further rise would re-ignite trade friction.
"The market was geared up for Rubin to talk a bit tougher on trade policy," said Nick Parsons, foreign exchange strategist at Banque Paribas.
Speaking in Hanoi, Rubin reiterated the dollar had been strong for "quite some time" and this had been helpful to the U.S. economy.
"I think that the strength of the dollar that we've had for quite some time now has spurred low interest rates, low rates of inflation...in the United States," he said.
"Having said that, I am not expressing any view...with regard to the level or direction that we would seek one way or another."
The Japan-U.S. surplus made the market wary of verbal intervention by Rubin to stem dollar strength.

Japan's current account surplus rose in February for the second month in a row, although dollar markets shrugged it off and instead moved higher. Tokyo's surplus in its current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, rose 15.4 percent to 865.2 billion yen ($6.92 billion) in February from a year earlier, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) announced on Monday.
The surplus was slightly above economists' average forecast of 801.1 billion yen ($6.40 billion) and follows a rise in January, the first in 17 months.
Analysts said the dollar got a leg-up against the mark as the odds in favour of European Monetary Union (EMU) increased.

Positive EMU sentiment rose after a weekend meeting of European finance ministers in the Netherlands set Spring 1988 as the date for deciding on the first wave of EMU participants as well as agreeing details of stability pact fines and sanctions.
Agreement was also reached on a new Exchange Rate Mechanism linking the euro to those outside the first-wave.

"Threshing out details that needed sorting out, in particularly on when and for how long EMU fines will be applicable, has lifted the overall impression of uncertainty hanging over the single currency," Credit Lyonnais economist David Thwaites said.
